A common API does not mean identical latency, caching, persistence, or failure behavior underneath.

the-vfs-layer.title: A mount connects another filesystem into the namespace
the-vfs-layer.body: Path traversal can cross a mount point and begin resolving entries in a different filesystem. The mounted object can hide entries that existed at that path in the underlying tree until the mount is removed. Bind mounts and mount namespaces further change what a process sees. Diagnose paths from the affected process's mount view rather than assuming the host's view is identical.

the-vfs-layer.title: Pseudo filesystems expose generated information
the-vfs-layer.body: Some file-like interfaces generate data from kernel state instead of retrieving ordinary stored file bytes. Reported size, seek support, and read behavior can differ from regular files. A single read may return a snapshot or a portion of generated text according to the interface. Treat documented semantics as authoritative instead of assuming a device, process-information file, and disk file behave identically.

the-vfs-layer.title: Network filesystems introduce remote failure boundaries
the-vfs-layer.body: An operation can wait on a remote server, observe cache validation behavior, or fail after a network interruption. Local descriptor validity does not prove the remote operation completed. File locking and persistence semantics can depend on the protocol and configuration. A filesystem abstraction simplifies programming, but recovery logic must still account for the failure and consistency contract of the selected backing service.

file-allocation-and-extents.title: Contiguous, linked, and indexed layouts solve different problems
file-allocation-and-extents.body: A contiguous layout records a start and length, making sequential access simple but growth difficult. Linked allocation follows block pointers, which complicates random access. Indexed structures locate blocks through metadata and support more flexible placement. Real filesystems use richer designs, but these basic models explain why metadata lookup, fragmentation, and growth costs differ even for files with equal byte lengths.

file-allocation-and-extents.title: Extents compress runs of consecutive allocation
file-allocation-and-extents.body: An extent describes a range of logical file blocks mapped to a consecutive storage range. A 1,000-block run can be represented much more compactly than 1,000 individual block pointers. Fragmented files need more extents and metadata traversal. Physical adjacency can help some storage workloads, but an extent is a mapping representation, not a guarantee of one device request or equal latency on every medium.

file-allocation-and-extents.title: Sparse holes read as zeros without equivalent allocated storage
file-allocation-and-extents.body: A file can have a large logical size with ranges that have no ordinary data blocks allocated. Reading a hole returns zeros under regular sparse-file semantics. Copying the bytes naively can materialize those zeros and consume much more storage at the destination. Compare logical size with allocated blocks, and choose copying tools that preserve holes when that property matters.

file-allocation-and-extents.title: Preallocation changes when allocation failures occur
file-allocation-and-extents.body: Reserving storage in advance can reduce later fragmentation and make some out-of-space failures occur before a critical write path. The exact guarantee depends on the allocation operation and filesystem. It does not ensure future writes are durable or eliminate device errors. State whether the goal is physical reservation, logical file growth, or initialization, because these are distinct operations.

dentry-and-inode-caches.title: Name lookup and file content use different caches
dentry-and-inode-caches.body: A dentry cache remembers name-to-object lookup relationships, while inode caches retain object metadata. The page cache holds file content pages. A workload repeatedly checking whether files exist can stress lookup and metadata without reading much content. Dropping or warming only file data does not necessarily reproduce a cold pathname lookup, so benchmark setup must specify which caches matter.

dentry-and-inode-caches.title: Negative lookup caching avoids repeated failed searches
dentry-and-inode-caches.body: A cached negative lookup records that a name was not found under the relevant context and validity rules. Repeated attempts to open a missing configuration file can then avoid some underlying lookup work. Creation, invalidation, and remote consistency require appropriate updates. A cached absence is not a timeless truth; its usefulness depends on knowing when the namespace may have changed.

dentry-and-inode-caches.title: References constrain which cached objects can be reclaimed
dentry-and-inode-caches.body: Cached metadata may be reclaimable when unused, but active references and filesystem rules can keep objects alive. A growing metadata cache is not automatically a leak. Correlate its growth with directory traversal, file counts, and memory pressure, then see whether reclaim occurs. Repeatedly scanning millions of names can consume substantial metadata memory even when the application retains no file payload.

dentry-and-inode-caches.title: Cold and warm traversal measure different workloads
dentry-and-inode-caches.body: The first walk of a directory tree can need metadata reads and object creation, while a repeated walk may use cached relationships. Report both when evaluating startup or backup behavior. Changing only the application process does not necessarily clear kernel caches. A benchmark that restarts the process but retains warm filesystem metadata can seriously understate a fresh machine's traversal latency.

crash-consistency.title: Define invariants that must survive an interrupted update
crash-consistency.body: Creating a file can involve allocation metadata, an inode, directory entries, and data blocks. A crash between updates can leave references to uninitialized content or allocated storage with no reachable owner unless the filesystem protects its invariants. Application consistency adds another layer: two individually valid files can disagree about one transaction. State both filesystem and application invariants before designing recovery.

crash-consistency.title: Ordering must reach storage, not only the CPU instruction stream
crash-consistency.body: The application issues operations in one order, but caches, write-back, and devices can delay or reorder persistence within their contracts. A source-code sequence of write A then write B does not alone prove A survives whenever B survives. Persistence barriers and synchronization operations establish relevant boundaries. Memory-ordering fences used between CPU threads solve a different problem from durable storage ordering.

crash-consistency.title: An atomic replacement needs a persistence protocol
crash-consistency.body: A common local-filesystem pattern writes a temporary file in the destination directory, synchronizes its contents, renames it over the destination, and synchronizes the directory when the platform requires that for durable naming. Check every result and account for filesystem-specific guarantees. The rename's concurrent visibility property and the directory entry's survival after a crash are separate parts of this protocol.

crash-consistency.title: Test crashes at every publication boundary
crash-consistency.body: A normal exit tests cleanup, not arbitrary interruption. Construct a disposable test that stops between content creation, synchronization, rename, and directory synchronization, then validates allowed recovery states. Include storage errors where possible. The goal is that recovered state belongs to a documented set, such as complete old version or complete new version, rather than merely that the program often appears to work.

journaling.title: A transaction records enough information for recovery
journaling.body: A journaling filesystem groups selected changes into transactions and writes a log describing them before treating the update as committed under its design. Recovery identifies complete committed transactions and applies or replays the necessary work. Incomplete transactions must not be mistaken for valid committed state. Sequence numbers, checksums, and commit markers help distinguish log boundaries and damaged or stale records.

journaling.title: Commit and checkpoint are different phases
journaling.body: Committing makes the journal transaction recoverable according to the persistence protocol. Checkpointing later places updates in their final home locations and allows old log space to be reused. A crash after commit but before checkpoint can be handled by replay. Confusing these phases leads to assuming the final filesystem blocks must already contain every committed update when the application receives success.

journaling.title: Metadata journaling does not automatically journal file contents
journaling.body: Some modes protect filesystem metadata while ordering or handling ordinary file data separately; other modes journal more data at additional write cost. Consequently, a structurally consistent filesystem can still contain an old or incomplete application record after a crash. Choose the application's synchronization protocol explicitly. The presence of a journal is not a substitute for checking the content durability guarantee.

journaling.title: Journal capacity and transaction size affect performance
journaling.body: If the log fills faster than transactions can checkpoint, new work may wait for space even when the device has unused bandwidth at other moments. Large transactions can increase batching efficiency but extend wait or recovery work. Measure synchronization latency and transaction behavior under sustained load. A fast short benchmark can finish before log pressure exposes the workload's true steady-state limit.

copy-on-write-file-systems.title: New blocks preserve the old reachable version
copy-on-write-file-systems.body: Instead of overwriting every live block in place, a copy-on-write filesystem writes new content and the metadata path needed to reference it. Publication changes which root or committed metadata version is authoritative under the filesystem's transaction rules. Old reachable blocks remain available until no retained version needs them. This strategy supports snapshots but still requires correct ordering and crash-recovery design.

copy-on-write-file-systems.title: Snapshots retain references rather than making immediate full copies
copy-on-write-file-systems.body: A snapshot can initially share most blocks with the live filesystem. Subsequent writes allocate replacement blocks while the snapshot retains old versions. The apparent snapshot creation cost can be small, but later changes consume space. Deleting a large file from the live view may reclaim little while snapshots still reference its blocks, so capacity planning must include retained versions.

copy-on-write-file-systems.title: Checksums detect corruption only within their defined coverage
copy-on-write-file-systems.body: Some copy-on-write filesystems combine checksums with redundancy to detect and potentially repair damaged data. Copy-on-write alone does not imply checksumming or automatic repair. A checksum can identify inconsistency but needs a valid alternative copy or recovery source to restore content. Understand which metadata and data are protected, and test scrubbing and recovery procedures instead of assuming every corruption is self-healing.

copy-on-write-file-systems.title: Write amplification and fragmentation are trade-offs
copy-on-write-file-systems.body: A small logical update can require new data blocks and several metadata blocks, especially with snapshots and deep trees. Repeated updates may reduce physical locality or increase space pressure. Workload, filesystem design, and tuning determine the effect. Compare sustained throughput, synchronization latency, and allocated space over time rather than judging only the speed of a fresh empty filesystem.

storage-hardware.title: HDD latency combines positioning and transfer
storage-hardware.body: A hard disk may need to move its head to a track and wait for rotation before transferring bytes. Sequential access amortizes those positioning costs across a run, while small random requests repeatedly pay them. Queue reordering can improve locality but add waiting. A disk's advertised sequential bandwidth therefore does not predict its small random-operation throughput or tail latency.

storage-hardware.title: Flash writes and erases use different granularities
storage-hardware.body: An SSD programs and erases flash under device-specific constraints, commonly with erase units larger than an application write. Its translation layer maps logical blocks to physical flash and performs garbage collection and wear management. Updating a small logical range can cause additional internal copying. Sustained performance can differ from a short test that fits in a cache or begins with abundant free blocks.

storage-hardware.title: NVMe changes the host-device interface
storage-hardware.body: NVMe provides an interface designed for nonvolatile storage with multiple queues and efficient command processing. It is not itself a guarantee that every device is faster for every workload. Media, controller, firmware, queue depth, and power policy still matter. Distinguish the transport and command interface from the storage medium when comparing SATA SSDs, NVMe SSDs, and network-attached storage.

storage-hardware.title: Volatile caches affect what completion means
storage-hardware.body: A controller can acknowledge a write after accepting it into a cache that may or may not survive power loss. Flush and force-unit-access mechanisms, power-loss protection, and truthful device behavior influence durability. An application cannot infer these properties from throughput alone. Describe the full storage stack, including virtual disks and controllers, when making claims about surviving a particular failure.

storage-performance.title: Convert operation rate into transferred bytes
storage-performance.body: At 10,000 operations per second with 4 KiB transferred per operation, payload bandwidth is approximately 39.1 MiB per second. At the same operation count with 1 MiB operations, the bandwidth demand is entirely different. Always report request size and read/write mix alongside IOPS. A headline operation rate without those details cannot support a meaningful workload comparison.

storage-performance.title: Queue depth can expose parallelism and increase waiting
storage-performance.body: A device may need several requests in flight to use internal parallelism, but additional queue depth beyond saturation mainly increases waiting. In a stable approximation, outstanding requests equal completed requests per second multiplied by average response time. At 20,000 IOPS and 1 ms average response time, about twenty requests are outstanding. This includes queueing under the stated measurement boundary.

storage-performance.title: Percentiles reveal delays hidden by averages
storage-performance.body: Most reads can complete quickly while occasional garbage collection, synchronization, or contention produces long stalls. An average alone hides those events. Measure median and tail latency under sustained representative load, with the same durability settings used in production. A system that maximizes aggregate throughput can still violate an application's deadline on its slowest requests.

storage-performance.title: Control caches and test duration deliberately
storage-performance.body: A benchmark can accidentally measure RAM caching rather than the intended device, or finish before write-back catches up. State whether the workload is buffered, direct, synchronous, sequential, or random, and record warmup and runtime. Use a data set and method matching the question. Disabling caches indiscriminately can produce an artificial workload just as easily as leaving them warm.

disk-scheduling-algorithms.title: FCFS and shortest-seek-time-first choose different request order
disk-scheduling-algorithms.body: First-come, first-served honors arrival order and is simple to explain, but can cause large head movements on a disk. Shortest-seek-time-first chooses a nearby pending request, improving locality while risking starvation of distant requests under continuous nearby arrivals. Request ordering affects waiting distribution as well as aggregate movement; minimizing one does not automatically optimize fairness.

disk-scheduling-algorithms.title: SCAN and LOOK sweep in one direction
disk-scheduling-algorithms.body: SCAN services requests while moving in a direction, reaches the relevant boundary, then reverses. LOOK reverses at the furthest pending request rather than necessarily going to the physical end. State the initial head position, direction, request set, and boundary assumptions before calculating movement. Otherwise two different answers may reflect different models rather than arithmetic errors.

disk-scheduling-algorithms.title: Circular variants aim for more uniform directional service
disk-scheduling-algorithms.body: C-SCAN services in one direction and returns to the beginning without serving on the return, while C-LOOK limits the circular jump to the pending request range. Whether the return jump counts toward movement must be explicit in a classroom calculation. These policies trade seek distance against service regularity and are not interchangeable names for ordinary SCAN.

disk-scheduling-algorithms.title: A short worked movement comparison
disk-scheduling-algorithms.body: Start at cylinder 50 with pending requests 10, 20, and 90. FCFS in that order travels 40 + 10 + 70 = 120 cylinders. Shortest-seek-time-first chooses 20, then 10, then 90, traveling 30 + 10 + 80 = 120 as well. Equal totals on one trace do not make the policies equivalent. SSD scheduling has different concerns because mechanical seek is absent.

the-block-layer.title: File bytes become block requests through mappings
the-block-layer.body: The filesystem determines which logical storage blocks correspond to a file operation and submits work through the block stack. Requests can pass through partitioning, device mapping, encryption, redundancy, and driver queues. One application operation can become several lower-level requests, while adjacent work can sometimes merge. Do not expect application syscall counts to equal physical device-command counts.

the-block-layer.title: Merging saves overhead but has eligibility rules
the-block-layer.body: Adjacent requests may be combined when direction, device, limits, and other attributes permit. Larger combined operations can reduce command overhead and improve sequential efficiency. Device transfer limits can also split a large request. Trace the specific queue boundary when investigating request sizes; a large application buffer can still produce several commands after filesystem mapping or device-limit processing.

the-block-layer.title: Multiple queues change where contention occurs
the-block-layer.body: Modern block stacks can use several software and hardware submission queues to reduce shared locking and exploit device parallelism. CPU placement and queue mapping influence contention. More queues do not create unlimited media capacity, and completion processing still consumes CPU. Separate time waiting in software from time reported at the device before selecting a scheduler or changing queue limits.

the-block-layer.title: Flush and discard are not ordinary payload writes
the-block-layer.body: A flush establishes persistence-related behavior through the supported stack, while discard communicates that selected logical storage ranges are no longer needed. Their semantics differ from reading or writing application bytes. Layers must correctly propagate the operations they promise to support. An optimization that drops ordering or flush requirements can make a fast benchmark incompatible with the application's durability contract.

the-page-cache.title: File-backed cache pages can serve multiple readers
the-page-cache.body: The page cache associates cached contents with backing file positions, allowing repeated reads and compatible mappings to reuse resident data. A second process can benefit from pages loaded by the first. Restarting an application does not necessarily make its file access cold. Distinguish process-local caches from the kernel's shared file cache when interpreting benchmark or memory behavior.

the-page-cache.title: Dirty pages carry an obligation to preserve changed data
the-page-cache.body: A buffered write modifies cached pages and marks them dirty. Write-back later sends changes toward storage, while concurrent modifications can complicate which version is considered clean. Dirty limits prevent unbounded accumulation and can throttle writers. A large apparent burst throughput can be borrowing RAM capacity; sustainable throughput requires write-back to keep pace over time.

the-page-cache.title: Reclaim treats clean and dirty cache differently
the-page-cache.body: A clean file-backed page can often be discarded because its contents remain available from the file. A dirty page requires write-back or another valid preservation action before its memory is reused. Thus equal cache sizes can represent different reclaim costs. When memory pressure stalls a writer, inspect dirty and write-back activity rather than assuming every cached page is instantly disposable.

the-page-cache.title: Cache coherence does not imply durable persistence
the-page-cache.body: A reader may observe bytes another process wrote through the cache while those bytes remain vulnerable to a system crash. This is ordinary visibility through a coherent file view, not proof of persistence. Synchronization operations establish a different guarantee. Explain which observer and failure scenario a test covers; reading back data successfully on the same running machine is not a crash-durability test.

buffered-and-direct-io.title: Buffered I/O trades copies and caching for reuse
buffered-and-direct-io.body: Buffered access commonly copies through the page cache, enabling repeated reads, readahead, and deferred writes. This can greatly help reused data but may duplicate caching already performed by a database. Copies are only one cost among allocation, faults, locks, and storage waits. Measure the whole path before assuming bypassing the page cache automatically lowers latency.

buffered-and-direct-io.title: Direct I/O has alignment and support constraints
buffered-and-direct-io.body: Direct I/O requests attempt to bypass relevant page-cache paths under filesystem and platform rules. Buffer address, transfer length, and file offset may need particular alignment, and support varies. Invalid requests can fail or behave according to documented fallback rules. Discover the actual contract for the target filesystem instead of hard-coding one universal alignment value for every device and kernel.

buffered-and-direct-io.title: Direct does not mean synchronous or durable
buffered-and-direct-io.body: A direct write can avoid a particular cache while still completing before the required persistence boundary unless the selected flags and synchronization establish it. Directness concerns the data path, synchrony concerns waiting, and durability concerns survival. These are independent questions. A database using direct I/O still needs a correct log and synchronization protocol for committed transactions.

buffered-and-direct-io.title: Mixed access modes require coherence-aware design
buffered-and-direct-io.body: Accessing overlapping file ranges through buffered, direct, and mapped paths can create additional coherence work and restrictions. Filesystem implementations differ, so avoid assuming the cheapest independent behavior of each path composes automatically. Prefer a documented access pattern and benchmark it as a whole. Account for cache invalidation and synchronization when switching modes during a test.

durability-and-fsync.title: Distinguish language flush, kernel acceptance, and durable completion
durability-and-fsync.body: Flushing a language stream usually pushes buffered bytes toward operating-system calls. A successful write can still leave data in volatile kernel or device buffers. A suitable synchronization operation requests the persistence guarantee of its platform and storage stack. These milestones must be named separately in a transaction protocol, especially when the application sends a success response before final synchronization.

durability-and-fsync.title: fsync and fdatasync differ in metadata scope
durability-and-fsync.body: On Linux, fsync synchronizes a file's changed data and associated metadata, while fdatasync can omit metadata not necessary for subsequent data retrieval. File-size information can still be necessary. Neither operation should be treated as a generic instruction to persist every directory entry referring to the file. Consult the actual filesystem and platform contract for naming changes and special file types.

durability-and-fsync.title: Persist newly published names through their directory
durability-and-fsync.body: A newly created or renamed file involves both the file object's contents and a directory entry. A durable replacement protocol commonly synchronizes the new file, performs the rename, and synchronizes the parent directory as required. If source and destination directories differ, reason about both. Check return values at every stage; a failed synchronization cannot be silently upgraded to durable success.

durability-and-fsync.title: Group commit amortizes persistence without weakening acknowledgments
durability-and-fsync.body: Suppose one flush takes 2 ms. Flushing every tiny record separately caps a serial path near 500 flushes per second, while batching twenty records can amortize that cost across them. The batch members must wait for the shared persistence boundary before receiving durable acknowledgment. Batching changes latency and throughput trade-offs, but acknowledging before the flush would change the guarantee itself.

raid.title: RAID 0 stripes without redundancy
raid.body: With N equal disks of capacity S, RAID 0 offers roughly N times S usable capacity by distributing data across disks. Parallelism can improve throughput, but losing one member can lose parts of the entire striped data set. Striping is not fault tolerance. Report stripe size and workload when discussing performance; a small request need not use every disk simultaneously.

raid.title: RAID 1 mirrors copies of the same data
raid.body: A simple two-disk mirror provides roughly one disk's usable capacity and can survive one member failing if the remaining copy is sound. Writes must maintain the mirror's required copies, while reads may be distributed according to implementation. Mirroring also reproduces logical deletions and corrupt application writes. It protects selected hardware failures, not an operator removing the wrong directory.

raid.title: RAID 5 uses one parity block per stripe
raid.body: Across N equal members, RAID 5 provides roughly (N − 1) times S usable capacity and tolerates one member failure. Parity is distributed across members rather than requiring one dedicated parity disk. A small update can require reading old data and parity before writing replacements, although implementations optimize particular cases. Degraded reads and rebuilds impose additional work and vulnerability.

raid.title: RAID 6 adds a second independent parity relationship
raid.body: RAID 6 provides roughly (N − 2) times S usable capacity and tolerates two member failures under its design. Its extra parity costs capacity and update work but extends protection during failures and rebuilding. It does not imply immunity to correlated faults, unreadable data beyond the protection budget, or software errors. Verify array health and backups rather than using parity count as a complete reliability estimate.

raid.title: RAID 10 stripes across mirrored groups
raid.body: In a common even-member layout, RAID 10 mirrors pairs and stripes across those pairs, yielding roughly half raw capacity. It can survive multiple failures if they do not remove every copy within the same mirror group. Two failures in different pairs differ from two failures in one pair. State the actual layout before claiming a fixed number of failures is always safe.

raid.title: Rebuild time and write ordering are operational concerns
raid.body: Rebuilding reads surviving data and writes a replacement while normal traffic may continue. Large members, heavy load, and additional errors extend exposure. Parity updates also require protection against interrupted multi-member writes, using mechanisms appropriate to the implementation. Monitor rebuild progress, test restoration from independent backups, and document controller cache protection; RAID availability is only one part of recoverability.

diagnosing-io-problems.title: Separate storage capacity from service capacity
diagnosing-io-problems.body: A volume can have free space yet be unable to serve the requested operation rate promptly. Conversely, a mostly idle device can reject writes because bytes, metadata objects, or quotas are exhausted. Capture the exact error or latency symptom first. A dashboard showing free gigabytes cannot answer whether synchronization latency or a per-user quota is causing failures.

diagnosing-io-problems.title: Correlate application waits with device evidence
diagnosing-io-problems.body: Measure the application's read, write, and synchronization durations, then compare device queueing, transfer sizes, and completion rates over the same interval. Long application waits with modest device activity can indicate locks, remote storage, metadata work, or throttling. Device busy time alone is not a universal saturation metric across modern parallel storage; interpret it with latency and throughput.

diagnosing-io-problems.title: Find which workload creates the requests
diagnosing-io-problems.body: Aggregate device activity can combine unrelated services, background write-back, backups, and filesystem maintenance. Attribute I/O to processes or groups where the platform permits, while recognizing that delayed kernel write-back can separate the issuing process from later device activity. Record file paths and operation types carefully. Reducing one application's reads may not help if the dominant pressure is another workload's writes.

diagnosing-io-problems.title: Change one variable and retain a recovery path
diagnosing-io-problems.body: Compare the same workload before and after changing batch size, synchronization frequency, access pattern, or storage placement. Preserve the required durability guarantee when evaluating performance. A faster configuration that loses acknowledged data is not an equivalent improvement. Use a disposable representative data set and repeat long enough to include cache draining, background work, and steady-state device behavior.
